previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: An elderly woman with a history of transfusion-dependent anemia, likely myelodysplastic syndrome, chronic diastolic heart failure, and long-term anticoagulation presented with diffuse abdominal pain when her hemoglobin dropped to 5.8 g/dL. She received one unit of packed red blood cells, after which her pain resolved, consistent with prior episodes. A CT scan showed no acute abdominal pathology, and lung findings initially concerning for pneumonia were reinterpreted as chronic lung changes, with a follow-up CT chest recommended in three months. Her hyponatremia improved without intervention, and she was discharged home the same day in stable condition with plans for outpatient monitoring of INR, sodium, and blood counts, and resumption of her home medications including warfarin and furosemide.

Brief Hospital Course:
___ is a ___ with history of transfusion-dependent 
anemia secondary to presumed myelodysplastic syndrome, 
diverticulosis, gastritis, and chronic abdominal pain who 
presented with worsening of her chronic abdominal pain and was 
found to have Hgb 6.1.

# Anemia: Patient had note in OMR documenting a Hgb of 7.9 from 
___ (2 days prior to admission). She was last transfused 2 
weeks prior to admission. In the ED she was noted to have brown 
stool that was guaiac positive. Both the patient and her 
caregiver denied any dark or bloody stools. Of note, her INR was 
4.2 (on warfarin for history of PE/DVT). She does have known 
gastritis and erosions as well as diverticulosis. Given the 
rapidity of the drop, it was concerning for a GI bleed, but she 
reported no such bleed and had no evidence of melena during this 
hospitalization. She responded appropriately to transfusion and 
Hgb remained stable the following afternoon. Despite our 
recommendations, the patient and her son/HCP were not interested 
in additional work up for GI bleeding. Her PO omeprazole was 
increased from 20 mg to 40 mg BID on discharge.  She was 
discharged with recommendation to follow up with hematology. 

# Abdominal pain: The patient described LUQ abdominal pain 
similar to her chronic abdominal pain. She and her son said her 
chronic abdominal pain worsens in the setting of anemia and 
declined CT in the ED. Her pain was improved but still present 
after transfusion.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Ms. ___,

You were hospitalized at ___ 
because you had worsening of your abdominal pain and you were 
found to be anemic (to have a low blood cell count). Your low 
blood cell count is likely in part due to your myelodysplastic 
syndrome, which means that your body does not produce blood 
cells well. You may also have some slow amount of bleeding from 
your stomach or intestines as well but this is likely not 
happening a lot right now. 

We have increased the dose of your omeprazole from 20 mg to 40 
mg to minimize damage to your stomach and bleeding. This damage 
may be the cause of your abdominal pain.

You should come back to the hospital if you have any blood in 
your stool or vomiting of blood. You should also return if you 
feel dizzy or lightheaded.

Being on the blood thinner, warfarin, increases your risk of 
bleeding. We discussed stopping this medication, but you wanted 
to continue taking it. You may want to continue this discussion 
with your blood doctor, ___.

It was a pleasure participating in your care. We wish you all 
the best in the future.

Sincerely,

Your ___ team

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ with hypoxia, chronic interstitial lung disease, evaluate for
pneumonia.

TECHNIQUE:  Chest PA and lateral

COMPARISON:  Multiple prior chest radiographs dating back to ___
and chest CT dated ___

FINDINGS: 

Bibasilar interstitial opacities are similar to multiple prior studies with
decreased lung volumes causing bronchovascular crowding compared with the
immediate prior study.  There is no definite focal consolidation to suggest
interval pneumonia.  There is no pleural effusion, pneumothorax, or pulmonary
edema.  The cardiomediastinal silhouette is stable.

IMPRESSION: 

No definite acute cardiopulmonary process, although new superimposed pneumonia
is difficult to exclude in the setting of extensive chronic bibasilar
interstitial changes.
